1261.quote_or_event: “Looking for Him, my eyes have become blood-shot.”
1261.explanation: Kabir describes the seeker who has searched for the Lord so long and so hard that the eyes themselves are worn and reddened.
1261.tie_back: The wife in the Kural says her eyes have grown dim from watching the road for her husband; Kabir's eyes are likewise worn out by looking for the Beloved.
1261.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 341, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1261._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a close image of eyes worn out by searching for the beloved, though Kabir's longing is spiritual (for God), not romantic, and the Kural's detail of counting the days on the wall has no parallel.

1262.quote_or_event: “How could I forget Him from my mind, even for an instant? He is the Most Worthy; He is my very life!”
1262.explanation: Guru Arjan says that forgetting the Lord is unthinkable, because the Lord is the very life of the devotee.
1262.tie_back: The wife says that if she forgot her husband even now, her arms would lose their beauty; Guru Arjan likewise cannot imagine forgetting the Beloved who is his life.
1262.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 80, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1262._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a good thematic fit on the impossibility of forgetting the beloved, but Gurbani's love is spiritual devotion to God, and the Kural's image of bangles slipping from wasted arms has no parallel here.

1263.quote_or_event: “Without Him, I cannot live, even for a moment. Without His Name, I die.”
1263.explanation: Guru Nanak says the soul's life depends entirely on the Lord; without Him there is only death.
1263.tie_back: The wife in the Kural lives on only because she longs for her husband's return; Guru Nanak too says life itself hangs on the Beloved.
1263.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 58, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1263._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both say life depends on the beloved, but the Kural's contrast between his desire for victory and her desire for his return is absent, and the love here is spiritual, not romantic.

1264.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the soul-bride is gazing upon Your Path; please listen, O Supreme Soul.”
1264.explanation: In the opening of his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Nanak pictures the soul-bride watching the road for her Husband Lord and begging Him to hear her.
1264.tie_back: The Kural's heart climbs from branch to branch to look out for the returning husband; Guru Nanak's soul-bride likewise keeps watch on the road for the Beloved.
1264.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1107, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1264._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a genuine bride-soul image of watching the road for the beloved's return, but it is spiritual longing for God, and the Kural's striking picture of the heart climbing a tree is not in it.

1265.quote_or_event: “Gazing upon my Beloved with my eyes, I have obtained all treasures;”
1265.explanation: Guru Arjan says that simply seeing the Beloved Lord with one's own eyes gives everything a person could want.
1265.tie_back: The wife says that once she sees her husband to her eyes' content, her paleness will vanish of itself; Guru Arjan likewise finds that the sight of the Beloved fulfils every lack.
1265.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 372, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1265._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a strong fit on the healing power of seeing the beloved (darshan), though the Beloved is God and the Kural's pallor of separation is not mentioned.

1266.quote_or_event: “The Dear Lord is the fruit-bearing tree; drinking in the Ambrosial Nectar, thirst is quenched.”
1266.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the Lord as a tree that gives nourishing fruit; drinking in His nectar ends the soul's thirst.
1266.tie_back: The Kural's wife wants to drink in her husband's presence until her sickness of longing is gone; Guru Amar Das likewise speaks of drinking in the Beloved's nectar until thirst is satisfied.
1266.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 114, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1266._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; the shared image of drinking in the beloved to end a painful thirst is strong, but Gurbani's nectar is the Lord's Name, a spiritual not romantic presence.

1267.quote_or_event: “whether your Lord and Master is angry with you or in love with you.”
1267.explanation: In this hymn Kabir speaks of the devotee's relationship with the Master as one that holds both displeasure and love.
1267.tie_back: The wife wonders whether, when her husband returns, she will sulk, embrace him, or both; Kabir's line likewise holds anger and love together in one bond.
1267.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 338, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1267._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match only: it pairs anger and love in a relationship with the Master, but here the anger is the Lord's, not the lover's playful sulk, and the Kural's comic indecision has no parallel.

1268.quote_or_event: “My sought-after Husband Lord has come home, and now, congratulations are pouring in.”
1268.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the joy of the soul-bride when the Husband Lord she longed for finally comes home, and everyone celebrates.
1268.tie_back: In the Kural the husband longs to finish the campaign and come home to feast with his wife; Guru Arjan pictures the happy homecoming itself and its celebration.
1268.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 704, Raag Jaithsree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1268._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; partial: it shares the joyful homecoming and celebration, but the Kural's speaker is the husband eager to return from war, whereas in Gurbani the bride (the soul) welcomes the Lord; the love is spiritual.

1269.quote_or_event: “With each and every breath, I think of You, day and night; I do not forget You, for an instant, even for a moment.”
1269.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind fixed on the Beloved through every breath, day and night.
1269.tie_back: The Kural says that for those whose minds are fixed on the day of the beloved's return, one day drags like seven; Guru Arjan likewise speaks of a mind that holds the Beloved in thought through every moment.
1269.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 247, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1269._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: it shares the mind fixed on the beloved through all time, but not the Kural's key point that waiting makes one day feel like seven; the love is spiritual.

1270.quote_or_event: “My Beloved has not come home, and I am dying of the sorrow of separation. The lightning flashes, and I am scared.”
1270.explanation: In his Barah Maha Guru Nanak's soul-bride says that while her Beloved stays away she is dying of the grief of separation.
1270.tie_back: The Kural's husband fears his wife will die of the grief of waiting, so that his return will come too late; Guru Nanak's soul-bride voices that very danger of dying while the Beloved is away.
1270.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1270._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a strong fit on dying of the grief of separation before the beloved returns, though the Kural's speaker is the husband and Gurbani's love is spiritual longing for God, not romantic.
